subject: literature
title: The First Gothic Novels, c. 1764–1820: haunted castles, trapped heroines and the birth of horror
dek: Between Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in 1764 and Charles Maturin's Melmoth the Wanderer in 1820, a cheap and much-mocked kind of novel filled with ruined abbeys, locked rooms, villainous monks and fainting heroines became the most popular fiction in Britain. Many of its best-selling authors and most of its readers were women, and in the hands of Ann Radcliffe, Mary Wollstonecraft and Mary Shelley the Gothic became a way of writing about fear, power, property and the female body that still shapes horror today.
era: c. 1764–1820, from The Castle of Otranto to Frankenstein and Melmoth the Wanderer, with roots in Burke's theory of the sublime and graveyard poetry, and an afterlife in the Brontës, Poe, Dracula, Rebecca and feminist criticism.
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in the English Wikipedia articles on Gothic fiction, The Castle of Otranto, Horace Walpole, Strawberry Hill House, Clara Reeve, Ann Radcliffe, The Mysteries of Udolpho, The Italian, The Monk, Matthew Lewis, Vathek, Caleb Williams, Maria: or, The Wrongs of Woman, Minerva Press, the Northanger 'horrid novels', Northanger Abbey, Frankenstein, the Villa Diodati, the Year Without a Summer, The Vampyre, Melmoth the Wanderer, Liaozhai Zhiyi and Ugetsu Monogatari, and on checks of publication details such as Radcliffe's fees and the Frankenstein print run. Quotations are given as they are commonly quoted; spelling and punctuation vary slightly between editions. It is text only today, with no images.

fun_fact.title: One rainy night, two monsters
fun_fact.text: In April 1815 the volcano Mount Tambora in present-day Indonesia erupted, and the ash it threw into the atmosphere made 1816 'the year without a summer' in Europe. Stuck indoors at the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva that June, Lord Byron suggested that each guest write a ghost story. Eighteen-year-old Mary Godwin, soon to be Mary Shelley, began what became Frankenstein. Byron's doctor, John Polidori, later turned a fragment Byron abandoned into 'The Vampyre', which the New Monthly Magazine printed on 1 April 1819 as 'A Tale by Lord Byron'. So the same rainy summer gave the world both the modern scientist's monster and the modern aristocratic vampire, the ancestor of Dracula.

sections.title: Ruins, graveyards and the pleasure of fear

blocks.text: In the middle of the eighteenth century, 'Gothic' was mostly an insult. It referred to the Goths who sacked Rome, and by extension to anything medieval, rough and unclassical: pointed arches, dark cathedrals, superstition and feudal lords. Educated taste preferred the balance and reason of Greek and Roman models, and the novels of the day, by writers such as Samuel Richardson and Henry Fielding, were set in recognisable modern England and aimed to be realistic and morally useful.

At the same time, a counter-taste was growing. The 'graveyard poets', such as Thomas Gray, whose Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard appeared in 1751, made melancholy, tombs and night into fashionable subjects. Collectors began buying medieval objects, and wealthy men built fake ruins in their gardens. The fake Scottish epic of 'Ossian', published by James Macpherson in the 1760s, made ancient bards and misty landscapes fashionable across Europe.

The most important idea came from the Irish philosopher Edmund Burke. In A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757), he separated the beautiful, which is small, smooth and pleasant, from the sublime, which is vast, dark, powerful and frightening. Burke argued that whatever excites ideas of pain and danger, so long as we are not actually in danger, produces the strongest emotion the mind is capable of feeling. This gave writers a respectable reason to frighten their readers on purpose.

sections.title: Horace Walpole's dream and The Castle of Otranto

blocks.text: Horace Walpole was the youngest son of Robert Walpole, usually counted as Britain's first prime minister. He was a member of parliament, a famous letter-writer and a collector, and from 1749 he turned a small house at Twickenham, west of London, into Strawberry Hill, a toy-like Gothic castle with battlements, stained glass and a library modelled on old tombs. The house helped launch the Gothic Revival in architecture.

In a letter to the antiquarian William Cole dated 9 March 1765, Walpole explained that in early June 1764 he had dreamed he was in an ancient castle and saw, on the uppermost banister of a great staircase, a gigantic hand in armour. That evening he began writing without knowing what he meant to say, and he finished the book in about two months. The Castle of Otranto came out on Christmas Eve 1764, dated 1765, in an edition of 500 copies.

The first edition pretended to be an English translation, by one 'William Marshal', of an Italian text by 'Onuphrio Muralto', supposedly printed in Naples in 1529. The story is deliberately wild. On his wedding day, Conrad, the son of Manfred, Prince of Otranto, is crushed to death by a giant helmet that falls from the sky. Manfred, desperate to keep his family's stolen title, decides to divorce his wife Hippolita and marry Conrad's bride, Isabella, who flees through the castle's underground passages. Portraits walk out of their frames, statues bleed and giant pieces of armour keep appearing until the castle collapses and the rightful heir is revealed.

The book sold well, and when Walpole admitted his authorship in the second edition of 1765 he added the subtitle 'A Gothic Story'. In the new preface he explained his aim: to combine the old romance, where anything could happen, with the modern novel, where characters behave like real people. Critics who had praised a medieval curiosity now attacked a modern fake, but the formula of an ancient building, a tyrant, a persecuted young woman, a hidden crime and a lost inheritance had been set.

sections.title: Ann Radcliffe and the female Gothic

blocks.text: Women took the form over almost at once. Clara Reeve published The Champion of Virtue in 1777, retitled The Old English Baron in 1778, and said openly that it was 'the literary offspring of The Castle of Otranto'. She kept a ghost but made it serve justice, and she cut what she saw as Walpole's absurdities. Sophia Lee's The Recess (1783–1785) imagined twin daughters secretly born to Mary, Queen of Scots, hidden in an underground refuge. Charlotte Smith mixed Gothic scenes into novels about poverty and bad marriages.

The most important of these writers was Ann Radcliffe. Born Ann Ward in London in 1764, the same year Otranto appeared, she married the journalist William Radcliffe and published five novels between 1789 and 1797. The Romance of the Forest (1791) made her famous, and The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) made her the best-paid novelist of the decade: her publishers, G. G. and J. Robinson, paid £500 for the copyright, an extraordinary sum at the time. For The Italian (1797) she received £800. Then she stopped publishing novels altogether, and lived quietly until her death in 1823, so quietly that rumours spread that she had gone mad from her own horrors.

In Udolpho, the orphaned heroine Emily St. Aubert is carried off by her aunt's sinister husband, Montoni, to a castle in the Apennines. She is trapped, pressured to sign over her property, and haunted by noises, disappearing people and a black veil in a remote chamber, behind which she glimpses something so terrible that she faints. Hundreds of pages later, the novel explains it: the figure behind the veil is a wax image of a decaying body, made as a religious penance. This method, in which every apparently supernatural event finally has a natural cause, is called the 'explained supernatural'.

Radcliffe also explained her own theory. In an essay, 'On the Supernatural in Poetry', published after her death in 1826, she wrote that terror and horror are 'so far opposite, that the first expands the soul, and awakens the faculties to a high degree of life; the other contracts, freezes, and nearly annihilates them'. Terror, for her, was suspense and uncertainty, the sublime feeling Burke described. Horror was the shock of seeing something disgusting. She preferred terror. In 1976 the critic Ellen Moers, in her book Literary Women, gave a name to what Radcliffe and her followers wrote: the 'Female Gothic', fiction in which a young woman, often an orphan with property, is imprisoned in a house controlled by a powerful man and must find her way through it. Read this way, the castle is a picture of the family and of marriage law, in which a wife's property and body belonged to her husband.

sections.title: Matthew Lewis's The Monk and the male Gothic

blocks.text: Matthew Gregory Lewis read Udolpho while working at the British embassy in The Hague, and, as he told his mother, wrote his own novel in about ten weeks. The Monk appeared in 1796, when he was about twenty. It tells the story of Ambrosio, a famously holy abbot in Madrid, who is seduced by Matilda, a woman who entered his monastery disguised as a novice. Step by step he falls into rape, incest and murder, and at the end he sells his soul to the Devil, who drops him from a great height onto rocks. Interwoven with this are a bleeding nun, the Wandering Jew and a pregnant nun imprisoned in a crypt.

Unlike Radcliffe, Lewis showed everything and explained nothing: the ghosts and demons are real, and the violence is described in detail. Readers loved it, and 'Monk' Lewis became his nickname, but the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge, reviewing it in 1797, called it a book a parent might tremble to find in a son's or daughter's hands. Once people realised its author sat in Parliament, there was talk of legal action for blasphemy and obscenity, and Lewis toned down later editions. Critics now often contrast this 'male Gothic', with its explicit horror and its interest in the transgressor's mind, with Radcliffe's 'female Gothic' of terror and survival.

Radcliffe's reply was The Italian (1797), set in Naples in the 1750s. Its villain is again a monk, the brooding Schedoni, and its heroine, Ellena, is kidnapped and imprisoned in a convent and nearly murdered, but Radcliffe brought back suspense and restraint. Other notable men's Gothic novels of the period include William Beckford's Vathek (1786), an Orientalist tale of a caliph who seeks forbidden knowledge, and William Godwin's Caleb Williams (1794), in which a servant who discovers his master's crime is hunted across England, a Gothic plot used to attack the power of the rich.

sections.title: Minerva Press, circulating libraries and 'horrid novels'

blocks.text: The Gothic boom was also a business story. Novels were expensive, so most readers rented them from circulating libraries. William Lane's Minerva Press, named in 1790 and based in Leadenhall Street in London, published huge numbers of cheap novels, many of them Gothic and many by women, and supplied libraries across the country. Critics sneered at 'Minerva novels' and at their mostly female readers, and the stereotype of the silly young woman ruined by romances became a stock joke.

Jane Austen made that joke the subject of Northanger Abbey. In it, Isabella Thorpe gives her friend Catherine Morland a list of seven 'horrid' novels to read after Udolpho, including Eliza Parsons's Castle of Wolfenbach and The Mysterious Warning, Regina Maria Roche's Clermont, The Necromancer of the Black Forest, The Midnight Bell, The Orphan of the Rhine and Horrid Mysteries. For a long time readers assumed Austen invented the titles. In the 1920s the scholar Michael Sadleir and others showed that all seven were real books, several of them translated or adapted from German.

Austen wrote the novel around 1798–1799 and sold it, under the title Susan, to Crosby & Co. in 1803 for £10. Crosby never published it, and in 1816 her brother Henry bought it back for the same £10. It finally appeared after her death, together with Persuasion, at the end of 1817 in a set dated 1818. When Catherine visits the Tilney family's abbey, she imagines that General Tilney murdered his wife. She is wrong, and humiliated. But the general is a real bully who throws her out of the house when he learns she has no fortune, so Austen's joke also says that the Gothic was right about money and male power, if not about ghosts.

sections.title: Wollstonecraft's Maria: the asylum as the real castle

blocks.text: The Gothic grew up in the age of the French Revolution, and writers on both sides used it. Burke, now attacking the Revolution, described the mob invading Versailles in Gothic language. Radicals answered in kind. Godwin's Caleb Williams was subtitled Things as They Are. His partner Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), left unfinished at her death in 1797 a novel called Maria: or, The Wrongs of Woman, published by Godwin in 1798.

Maria opens in a private madhouse, where the heroine has been locked up by her husband, who wants her money and has taken her baby. She befriends her keeper, Jemima, a working-class woman whose own life of abuse, prostitution and poverty Wollstonecraft tells in detail. There are no ghosts. The Gothic prison is a real institution, and the villain uses the law, not magic. Wollstonecraft wrote in her preface that she wanted to show 'the misery and oppression, peculiar to women, that arise out of the partial laws and customs of society'. It is one of the clearest examples of how the Gothic's trapped heroine could become an argument about women's rights.

Wollstonecraft died eleven days after giving birth to a daughter, Mary. The girl grew up in Godwin's house surrounded by writers, and at sixteen she ran away with the married poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. In the summer of 1816 they stayed by Lake Geneva near Lord Byron, who had rented the Villa Diodati. It was the 'year without a summer', caused by the eruption of Mount Tambora the year before, and the cold, stormy weather kept the group indoors reading German ghost stories. Byron proposed that each write one.

In her introduction to the revised edition of 1831, Mary described how, after days of failing to think of anything, she lay awake and saw, as if in a waking dream, 'the pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together'. She began a short story and expanded it into a novel. Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus was published anonymously in three volumes on 1 January 1818, in 500 copies, with a preface by Percy. Many reviewers assumed a man had written it, and some guessed Percy himself. Her name appeared on the second edition of 1823.

The novel moves the Gothic out of the castle and into the laboratory. Victor Frankenstein, a young Genevan student, builds a man from parts of corpses and brings him to life, then runs away in disgust. The creature, abandoned, teaches himself to speak and read, is rejected by everyone he meets and turns to murder, demanding that Victor make him a mate. Victor begins, then tears the female creature apart, and the creature kills Victor's bride on their wedding night. Unlike the ghosts of Radcliffe or the devils of Lewis, the horror here is created by human science and human neglect, which is why Frankenstein is also often called the first science fiction novel.

Feminist critics have read it as a book about birth and motherhood written by a teenager who had lost her mother at birth and her own first baby in 1815, and about what happens when a man tries to create life without women. The creature's complaint, that he was made and then abandoned without love or a place in society, has been read as a story about orphans, slaves, the poor and anyone treated as a monster.

The Diodati contest produced a second classic. Byron began and abandoned a story about a mysterious aristocrat. His young doctor, John William Polidori, reworked it into 'The Vampyre', in which the cold, seductive Lord Ruthven, a portrait of Byron, drains the life of young women across Europe. The New Monthly Magazine printed it on 1 April 1819 as 'A Tale by Lord Byron', and it was a sensation, adapted for the stage in Paris and London. Polidori protested that the groundwork was Byron's but its development was his own. He died in 1821, aged twenty-five.

The Irish clergyman Charles Robert Maturin published Melmoth the Wanderer in 1820. Melmoth has sold his soul for an extra 150 years of life and can escape only if someone takes over his bargain, so he wanders through stories within stories, from a Spanish monastery under the Inquisition to an island in the Indian Ocean, offering the desperate a way out. Honoré de Balzac wrote a sequel, and Maturin's great-nephew Oscar Wilde used the name Sebastian Melmoth in exile after his release from prison. By the 1820s the fashion for long Gothic novels had faded, but the genre did not die. It moved into short stories, magazines, melodrama on stage and the novels of the next generation.

sections.title: What else was happening in the world at the same time

blocks.text: In Germany, a related fashion called the Schauerroman, or 'shudder novel', grew in the same decades. Friedrich Schiller's unfinished novel Der Geisterseher (The Ghost-Seer), serialised from 1787 to 1789, about a secret society manipulating a prince with fake apparitions, was hugely popular. German tales were translated into English, sometimes loosely, which is why several of Austen's 'horrid novels' have German roots. In the United States, Charles Brockden Brown published Wieland in 1798, a story of a family destroyed by voices that seem to come from God, which began the American Gothic tradition later continued by Edgar Allan Poe. In France the Marquis de Sade, in an essay of 1800, said the new novels of terror were the inevitable fruit of the revolutionary shocks that all of Europe had felt.

East Asia was having its own golden age of the supernatural story at exactly the same time. In China, Pu Songling (1640–1715) had spent decades writing nearly five hundred tales of fox spirits, ghost lovers and scholars visited by the dead, but Liaozhai Zhiyi (聊齋誌異, Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio) was first printed only in 1766, in the Qingke Pavilion (青柯亭) edition, two years after Otranto. Many of its stories are about women: fox and ghost women who are cleverer, freer and more loyal than the men they love. In Japan, Ueda Akinari's Ugetsu Monogatari (雨月物語, Tales of Moonlight and Rain), nine tales of ghosts, vengeful wives and possession adapted from Chinese and Japanese sources, was published in 1776. Kenji Mizoguchi's 1953 film Ugetsu later made two of its stories famous worldwide. And in 1791 the first printed version of Dream of the Red Chamber (紅樓夢), the Cheng–Gao edition, appeared in Beijing.

In Taiwan, then a frontier prefecture of the Qing empire, these were the years of rapid Han Chinese settlement and of the Lin Shuangwen rebellion of 1786–1788, one of the largest uprisings of Qing rule on the island. Stories of ghosts and spirits circulated mostly through temples, festivals such as the Ghost Month (中元), and oral tradition rather than printed fiction. The comparison is useful because it shows two different traditions arriving at the same image at the same time: the beautiful, dangerous supernatural woman, who in Britain was usually a victim to be rescued and in Pu Songling's China was often the hero of the story.

sections.title: From Jane Eyre to Rebecca and The Bloody Chamber

blocks.text: The Brontës grew up reading Gothic tales in magazines, and Jane Eyre, with its locked attic, its mysterious screams and its secret first wife, Bertha Mason, is a Gothic novel set in an English country house. Wuthering Heights turned the Gothic villain into a romantic hero. In the 1860s the 'sensation novels' of Wilkie Collins and Mary Elizabeth Braddon brought Gothic secrets into modern suburban homes. Later in the century came Sheridan Le Fanu's lesbian vampire story Carmilla (1872), Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890) and Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897), which owes a great deal to Polidori.

In the twentieth century the female Gothic returned in Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca (1938), in which a young second wife is haunted by the memory of the first, in Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House (1959), and in Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966), which tells the story of Bertha Mason from her own side. Angela Carter's The Bloody Chamber (1979) rewrote fairy tales such as Bluebeard as feminist Gothic. The same year, Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar's The Madwoman in the Attic argued that the imprisoned, raging woman is a figure for the woman writer herself. Today the Gothic lives on in horror film, in novels such as Silvia Moreno-Garcia's Mexican Gothic (2020), and in every story where a house holds a secret about the family inside it.

items: The Gothic began as a game, a fake medieval translation by a rich collector, but it quickly became a serious way of writing about power: who owns the house, who can lock the doors and who inherits.

Its central plot, a young woman trapped by a man who wants her property or her body, reflected real law. Before the Married Women's Property Acts, a wife's money belonged to her husband, and a family could confine a woman in a private madhouse with little oversight.
Women dominated the genre as writers and readers. Radcliffe was the best-paid novelist of the 1790s, and the mockery of 'Minerva novels' was partly mockery of women's reading itself.
Radcliffe's distinction between terror (suspense and the unknown) and horror (the shock of seeing) still describes the difference between a slow ghost story and a slasher film.
Frankenstein moved fear from the supernatural to human responsibility: the monster is what happens when someone creates a life and then refuses to care for it.
The same decades saw a parallel boom in supernatural fiction in China and Japan, where the ghost or fox woman was more often the heroine than the victim.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Wollstonecraft's Maria is a Gothic story without ghosts: a wife locked up by a husband who controls her money and her child, helped only by another woman who has suffered even worse. The organisations you are studying for cool dairy, such as the Garden of Hope and the Modern Women's Foundation, work with women in versions of that situation today, including economic abuse and fights over custody. If you wrote a short note for a cool dairy shop tag explaining why proceeds go to these groups, could a Gothic image, such as a locked door or a house with a secret, help a customer understand economic abuse in one sentence, or would it make a real problem feel like fiction?
